title-group.article-title: Weekly board-game sessions and loneliness in community-dwelling older adults

abstract.p: A randomised controlled trial of a twelve-week facilitated board-game group for older adults, with loneliness as the primary outcome.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Loneliness affects a substantial minority of older adults and is associated with poorer health outcomes[1]. Group activities have been proposed as a remedy.

sec.title: 2. Methods
sec.p: This was a two-arm parallel randomised controlled trial.

sec.title: 2.1. Participants
sec.p: We recruited 120 community-dwelling adults aged 65 to 89 from four municipal community centres. Exclusion criteria were diagnosed dementia and severe visual impairment.

sec.title: 2.2. Intervention
sec.p: Participants in the intervention arm attended a weekly ninety-minute facilitated session in which they played physical board games including Rummikub, dominoes and a modern cooperative tile-laying game. No digital games were used.

sec.title: 2.3. Outcome measures
sec.p: The primary outcome was the UCLA Loneliness Scale, version 3, administered at baseline and at twelve weeks. Secondary outcomes were the WHO-5 Wellbeing Index and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment.

sec.title: 2.4. Statistical analysis
sec.p: We fitted a linear mixed model with arm, time and their interaction as fixed effects and participant as a random intercept.

sec.title: 3. Results
sec.p: Loneliness scores fell by 4.2 points in the intervention arm and by 0.6 points in the control arm, a between-group difference of 3.6 points (95% CI 2.1 to 5.1, p < 0.001).

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: Regular face-to-face board-game play reduced self-reported loneliness in this sample.

sec.title: 4.1. Limitations
sec.p: Participants could not be blinded to allocation, and the follow-up period was short.

sec.title: Ringraziamenti
sec.p: We thank the staff of the participating community centres.
